lead: A power BJT, a power MOSFET and an IGBT are switches that the control terminal turns both on and off. The BJT is driven by base current, the MOSFET by gate voltage, and the IGBT has a MOSFET gate with a bipolar output. They differ in drop, speed and voltage range, so the converter's voltage, current and frequency decide the choice. The MOSFET's switching intervals underlie every switching-loss and gate-drive calculation. They fill power supplies, inverters, motor drives and chargers.
prereq: You need: the transistor regions (cut-off, active, saturation) and the MOSFET threshold voltage.

blocks.text: A power BJT is a vertical n<sup>+</sup> emitter, p base, n<sup>−</sup> drift, n<sup>+</sup> collector structure. Off, its base-emitter junction is reverse-biased; on, enough base current saturates it, with V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> about 1 V to 2 V. Its gain β = I<sub>C</sub> / I<sub>B</sub> is only 5 to 20, so a 50 A switch needs several amperes of base current all the time. Between active and hard saturation lies quasi-saturation, with a higher V<sub>CE</sub>.

Its weak point is second breakdown: current crowds into a hot spot, which takes still more current and fails, even below rated power, so the safe operating area (SOA) bounds the allowed V<sub>CE</sub>–I<sub>C</sub> path. Slow removal of stored charge limits it to about 20 kHz, and it is now rarely chosen.

sections.h3: Power MOSFET and its dynamic behaviour

blocks.text: A power MOSFET is a vertical n<sup>+</sup> source, p body, n<sup>−</sup> drift, n<sup>+</sup> drain structure with an insulated gate. A gate-source voltage above the threshold V<sub>GS(th)</sub> inverts the p body and the channel conducts. Only majority carriers flow, so it switches in tens of nanoseconds. On, it is a resistance R<sub>DS(on)</sub>, so P<sub>cond</sub> = I<sub>D,rms</sub>² R<sub>DS(on)</sub>. R<sub>DS(on)</sub> rises with temperature, which makes paralleling easy and removes second breakdown, and rises steeply with voltage rating, so silicon MOSFETs suit a few hundred volts (superjunction designs reach 600 V to 900 V). A body diode conducts reverse current.

The gate sees C<sub>gs</sub>, C<sub>gd</sub> (the Miller capacitance) and C<sub>ds</sub>; datasheets give C<sub>iss</sub> = C<sub>gs</sub> + C<sub>gd</sub>, C<sub>oss</sub> = C<sub>ds</sub> + C<sub>gd</sub>, C<sub>rss</sub> = C<sub>gd</sub> and a gate charge curve. With a clamped inductive load, turn-on has four intervals:

items: Turn-on delay t<sub>d(on)</sub>: v<sub>GS</sub> rises from 0 to V<sub>GS(th)</sub>.

Current rise t<sub>ri</sub>: v<sub>GS</sub> rises to the plateau V<sub>pl</sub>; i<sub>D</sub> rises to the load current while v<sub>DS</sub> stays at the supply voltage (the freewheeling diode still conducts).

Voltage fall t<sub>fv</sub> (Miller plateau): v<sub>GS</sub> stays flat at V<sub>pl</sub> while the gate current discharges C<sub>gd</sub>; v<sub>DS</sub> falls to nearly zero. The charge needed is Q<sub>gd</sub>, so t<sub>fv</sub> = Q<sub>gd</sub> / I<sub>g</sub>.
v<sub>GS</sub> rises to the drive voltage and R<sub>DS(on)</sub> reaches its final low value. Turn-off runs the same intervals backwards.

blocks.text: Switching loss happens in the current-rise and voltage-fall intervals; a stronger gate current shortens them.

An IGBT is a MOSFET structure with an extra p<sup>+</sup> layer at the collector. When it conducts, this layer injects holes into the drift region (conductivity modulation), so the drop is V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> ≈ 1.5 V to 2.5 V almost independent of voltage rating. Its equivalent circuit is a MOSFET supplying the base current of a p-n-p transistor. The gate voltage (about +15 V) is held on while it conducts, but charge flows only at the edges. At turn-off the stored holes give a tail current that adds loss and limits switching to about 20 kHz to 50 kHz. The layers also form a parasitic thyristor that excess current can latch on (latch-up). Most IGBTs come with an inverse diode.

blocks.text: For conduction alone, MOSFET loss I² R<sub>DS(on)</sub> is a parabola and IGBT loss about V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> I a straight line; they are equal at I = V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> / R<sub>DS(on)</sub>, and below that the MOSFET wins.

examples.question: A MOSFET with R<sub>DS(on)</sub> = 0.1 Ω and an IGBT with V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> = 2 V do the same job. Find the conduction loss of each at 5 A and at 50 A, and the current at which the losses are equal.
steps: MOSFET at 5 A: 5² × 0.1 = 2.5 W. IGBT at 5 A: 2 × 5 = 10 W. The MOSFET wins.
MOSFET at 50 A: 50² × 0.1 = 250 W. IGBT at 50 A: 2 × 50 = 100 W. The IGBT wins.
Equal losses: I² R<sub>DS(on)</sub> = V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> I gives I = 2 ÷ 0.1 = 20 A.
examples.answer: 2.5 W against 10 W at 5 A, 250 W against 100 W at 50 A; the crossover is 20 A.

examples.question: A MOSFET switches a 10 A clamped inductive load from 200 V at 100 kHz, with its gate driven from 0 to 12 V through 10 Ω in total. The datasheet gives V<sub>GS(th)</sub> = 4 V, plateau V<sub>pl</sub> = 6 V, gate charge to the plateau Q<sub>gs</sub> = 14 nC, Q<sub>gd</sub> = 18 nC and total Q<sub>g</sub> = 50 nC. Estimate t<sub>d(on)</sub>, t<sub>ri</sub>, t<sub>fv</sub>, the turn-on energy and loss, and the gate drive power.
steps: Before the plateau the gate acts as C<sub>iss</sub> ≈ Q<sub>gs</sub> / V<sub>pl</sub> = 14 nC ÷ 6 V = 2.33 nF, so τ = 10 Ω × 2.33 nF = 23.3 ns. v<sub>GS</sub> = 12(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>) reaches 4 V at t<sub>d(on)</sub> = 23.3 × ln 1.5 = 9.5 ns and 6 V at 23.3 × ln 2 = 16.2 ns, so t<sub>ri</sub> = 6.7 ns.
On the plateau: I<sub>g</sub> = (12 − 6) ÷ 10 = 0.6 A, so t<sub>fv</sub> = Q<sub>gd</sub> / I<sub>g</sub> = 18 nC ÷ 0.6 A = 30 ns.
Turn-on energy: E<sub>on</sub> ≈ ½ × 200 V × 10 A × (6.7 + 30) ns = 36.7 µJ; at 100 kHz, P<sub>on</sub> = 36.7 µJ × 100 000 = 3.67 W.
Gate drive power: Q<sub>g</sub> V<sub>drive</sub> f<sub>s</sub> = 50 nC × 12 V × 100 000 = 0.06 W.
examples.answer: t<sub>d(on)</sub> ≈ 9.5 ns, t<sub>ri</sub> ≈ 6.7 ns, t<sub>fv</sub> = 30 ns; E<sub>on</sub> ≈ 36.7 µJ (3.7 W at 100 kHz); gate power 60 mW. The Miller plateau takes most of the switching time.

traps: MOSFET conduction loss grows as I²: the 2.5 W at 5 A becomes 250 W at 50 A, not 25 W.
The gate of a MOSFET or IGBT draws current only at the edges, but the gate voltage must be held on throughout conduction.

Using C<sub>iss</sub> for the Miller plateau time: the plateau needs Q<sub>gd</sub> at the plateau current, t<sub>fv</sub> = Q<sub>gd</sub> / I<sub>g</sub> (30 ns in the example), not R C<sub>iss</sub>.

quiz.q: Name the control quantity of a power BJT, a power MOSFET and an IGBT.
quiz.a: BJT: base current. MOSFET: gate-source voltage. IGBT: gate-emitter voltage.

quiz.q: Define C<sub>iss</sub>, C<sub>oss</sub> and C<sub>rss</sub> of a MOSFET.
quiz.a: C<sub>iss</sub> = C<sub>gs</sub> + C<sub>gd</sub> (input), C<sub>oss</sub> = C<sub>ds</sub> + C<sub>gd</sub> (output), C<sub>rss</sub> = C<sub>gd</sub> (reverse transfer, the Miller capacitance).

quiz.q: What is the Miller plateau, and what happens to v<sub>DS</sub> during it?
quiz.a: The flat part of v<sub>GS</sub> during turn-on (or turn-off) while the gate current charges C<sub>gd</sub>; v<sub>DS</sub> falls (or rises) across the whole supply voltage during it. Its length is Q<sub>gd</sub> / I<sub>g</sub>.

quiz.q: A MOSFET with R<sub>DS(on)</sub> = 0.05 Ω carries 20 A. Find its conduction loss.
A MOSFET has Q<sub>gd</sub> = 12 nC. The gate drive is 12 V through 8 Ω and the plateau is 5 V. Find the voltage fall time.
Why does an IGBT have a tail current at turn-off, and what does it limit?
quiz.a: The conductivity-modulated drift region stores holes injected by the p<sup>+</sup> collector. When the MOS channel turns off, these holes must recombine, so the current decays slowly while the voltage is already high. This adds turn-off loss and limits the switching frequency to tens of kilohertz.

beyond: Not for the exam. Superjunction MOSFETs break the steep rise of R<sub>DS(on)</sub> with voltage, and trench field-stop IGBTs trade V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> against tail current. Search for ‘MOSFET gate charge curve’ and ‘superjunction MOSFET’.

figure.caption: MOSFET turn-on in worked example 2. The drain current rises while v<sub>DS</sub> is still 200 V; then the gate voltage stays on the 6 V Miller plateau for 30 ns while v<sub>DS</sub> falls.
